title: Self-Evaluation Improves Selective Generation in Large Language Models
research_question: Can an LLM's token-level self-evaluation of its own free-form answers provide better confidence signals for selective generation and abstention than ordinary sequence likelihood?
methodology: The authors transform free-form generation into token-level evaluation tasks using Sample and Select, which presents sampled responses as multiple-choice alternatives, and Sample and Eval, which asks whether an individual answer is correct. A hybrid method first selects an answer comparatively and then estimates its pointwise correctness, optionally subtracting confidence assigned to a 'None of the above' option. Confidence methods are evaluated with accuracy, Calibration-AUC, and Selective-AUC, where low-confidence outputs are increasingly abstained. Experiments use PaLM-2 Large and, where API log-probabilities permit, GPT-3 on TruthfulQA and a 1,000-example sample of TL;DR.

key_findings.finding: Raw sequence likelihood was a poor confidence signal for free-form generation and was negatively correlated with correctness on TruthfulQA in several settings.
Recasting answer assessment as token-level self-evaluation substantially improved confidence-quality ranking compared with sequence likelihood.
On PaLM-2 TruthfulQA, the hybrid method with a 'None of the above' option achieved a Calibration-AUC of 75.34 compared with 39.80 for raw sequence likelihood.
Allowing 'None of the above' gave the model an explicit signal for cases in which none of the sampled answers appeared correct and generally improved calibration without a large accuracy penalty.
The advantage of self-evaluation over sequence-level confidence also appeared on TL;DR summarization, although the improvements were smaller than on TruthfulQA.
key_findings.section: 4.3 Self-evaluation improves calibration on TL;DR summarization

key_findings.finding: Self-evaluation remained useful after a self-critique-and-revision stage, indicating that confidence estimation and answer revision supplied complementary benefits.
Self-evaluation increases inference cost because the model must perform one or two additional evaluation passes after generation.

limitations: The principal experiments rely on PaLM-2 Large, while GPT-3 results are incomplete because its API exposed only limited token log-probabilities.
GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 could not be evaluated because their APIs did not expose the required output log-probabilities at the time of the study.

TruthfulQA correctness is approximated by GPT-judge rather than newly collected human labels, and TL;DR quality is approximated by a reward model whose reported human-rating prediction accuracy is 71.34%.
Only 1,000 examples from the 15,240-example TL;DR test split were evaluated to reduce inference cost.
The method increases inference time by roughly one additional evaluation pass, or two for the hybrid procedure.
The confidence scores are evaluated primarily as ranking signals through AUC rather than as numerically calibrated probabilities.
The study does not directly evaluate robustness under temporal change, explicit out-of-distribution shifts, or changing evidence sources.
No paper-specific source-code release is identified in the full text.
raw_claims: The method converts free-form generation into token-level self-evaluation tasks.
Sample and Select asks the model to choose among several independently sampled answers.
Sample and Eval asks the model to judge whether a particular candidate answer is correct.
A 'None of the above' choice is used to expose uncertainty when all sampled answers may be wrong.
Sequence likelihood performed poorly as a predictor of free-form answer quality.
Self-evaluation confidence was more predictive of answer quality than sequence likelihood on TruthfulQA.
The same general calibration pattern was observed on TL;DR summarization.
Selective-AUC measures answer quality as increasingly low-confidence outputs are abstained.
The hybrid self-evaluation procedure requires additional model inference.
